remediation.title: Getting Help and Getting Things Done

questions.question: You pay at the market and the seller gives you a small paper that shows what you paid. What is it called?
questions.options: a letter | a label | a ticket | a receipt
questions.explanation: A receipt is the paper that proves what you paid. A ticket lets you travel or enter, a label is on a product, and a letter comes in the post.

questions.question: At a busy market stall, people stand in a line and wait their turn. What is that line called?
questions.options: an audience | a queue | a staff | a team
questions.explanation: A queue is a line of people waiting their turn. A team works together, an audience watches, and staff are the people who work somewhere.

questions.question: You call the clinic to book a time to see the doctor. What are you making?
questions.options: a complaint | an appointment | a receipt | a timetable
questions.explanation: A fixed time to see the doctor is an appointment. A timetable lists many times, and a complaint is what you make when something is wrong.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: The Body, Illness and the Clinic

questions.question: You try on a shirt in a shop and it is exactly the right size. Which word do you use?
questions.options: It returns. | It fits. | It folds. | It costs.
questions.explanation: When clothes are the right size for your body, they fit. If they do not fit, you can return them to the shop.

questions.question: At the station, where do you stand and wait for your train?
questions.options: at the roundabout | on the pavement | at the stall | on the platform
questions.explanation: Trains stop at a platform. A roundabout is on the road, the pavement is where you walk, and a stall is at the market.

questions.question: Which word means the money you receive each month for your work?
questions.options: price | fare | change | salary
questions.explanation: Your salary is the money your employer pays you. A fare is what you pay to travel, a price is what a thing costs, and change is the money you get back.

questions.question: Water is escaping from the pipe under your sink, drop by drop. What do you call the problem?
questions.options: a refund | a leak | a junction | a slice
questions.explanation: When water escapes from a pipe, that is a leak — a useful word when you call for a repair. A refund is money returned to you.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Getting Help and Getting Things Done

questions.question: Your colleague shares her lunch and always helps new staff. Which word describes her?
questions.options: rude | shy | lazy | generous
questions.explanation: A generous person gives and shares freely. Lazy means avoiding work, rude means not polite, and shy means quiet with new people.

questions.question: A sign on a work site says an area is ‘forbidden’. What does that mean?
questions.options: You must enter quickly. | It is free to enter. | You are not allowed to enter. | It is fresh and clean.
questions.correctAnswer: You are not allowed to enter.
questions.explanation: Forbidden means not allowed. Signs use it for places and actions that are against the rules, often for safety.

questions.question: Which word begins with the sound you make with your tongue between your teeth?
questions.options: see | three | free | tree
questions.explanation: Three starts with the ‘th’ sound — tongue between the teeth, air flowing out. Tree, free and see start with other sounds.

questions.question: Which word means to reach a place at the end of a journey?
questions.options: wake | catch | arrive | order
questions.explanation: You arrive when you reach a place. You catch a bus to travel, you wake in the morning, and you order food at a café.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: ‘My neighbours ______ from Kenya.’
questions.options: are | is | am | be
questions.explanation: Neighbours means more than one person, so the verb is are: they are, we are, you are. Is goes with he, she and it; am goes with I.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence about your home.
questions.options: There is two rooms in my flat. | There am two rooms in my flat. | There be two rooms in my flat. | There are two rooms in my flat.
questions.correctAnswer: There are two rooms in my flat.
questions.explanation: Two rooms is plural, so we say there are. For one thing we say there is: there is a table in the kitchen.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: ‘My daughter ______ English at school.’
questions.options: to learn | learns | learn | learning
questions.explanation: With he, she and it, the present simple verb takes an s: she learns, he works, it costs. I, you, we and they use the plain form.

questions.question: Choose the sentence with ‘always’ in the correct place.
questions.options: I always catch the early bus. | I am always catch the early bus. | I catch always the early bus. | I catch the early always bus.
questions.correctAnswer: I always catch the early bus.
questions.explanation: Words like always, usually and never go before the main verb: I always catch, she usually walks, they never arrive late.

questions.question: Your friend has a bad cough. Give advice: ‘You ______ see a doctor.’
questions.options: have | do | are | should
questions.explanation: Should is the advice word: you should see a doctor, you should rest. Have needs to — you have to see a doctor — and that sounds like a rule, not advice.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: The Body, Illness and the Clinic

questions.question: Choose the correct past form: ‘Yesterday I ______ my keys at work.’
questions.options: losing | lose | lost | losed
questions.explanation: Lose is irregular: the past is lost, not losed. Yesterday tells us the action is finished, so we need the past simple.

questions.question: You have decided to visit your family next month. What do you say?
questions.options: I am visit my family. | I going to visit my family. | I am going to visit my family. | I visit my family yesterday.
questions.correctAnswer: I am going to visit my family.
questions.explanation: For a decision about the future, use going to with the full pattern: am going to visit. The other sentences are missing a piece or use the wrong time.

questions.question: You want to know the price of something. Which question do you ask?
questions.options: How is it much? | How many is it? | What much is it? | How much is it?
questions.explanation: For a price, ask how much. How many is for counting things — how many tickets, how many bags.

questions.question: The sign says ‘No smoking’. Which sentence matches the sign?
questions.options: You have to smoke here. | You must not smoke here. | You can smoke here. | You should smoke here.
questions.explanation: No smoking means the action is not allowed: you must not smoke. Must not is the strong form signs and rules use.

questions.question: You are at the ticket window at the station. Which is the polite, correct way to ask?
questions.options: I am like a single ticket. | I wanting a single ticket. | I would like a single ticket, please. | Me a single ticket.
questions.correctAnswer: I would like a single ticket, please.
questions.explanation: I would like is the polite pattern for asking for something: I would like a ticket, I would like an appointment. Adding please makes it warmer still.

questions.question: Read the recipe: ‘First, wash the rice. Then, boil the water. After that, add the rice.’ What do you do first?
questions.options: Wash the rice. | Add the rice. | Boil the water. | Serve the rice.
questions.explanation: The words first, then and after that show the order. First comes washing the rice, then boiling the water.

questions.question: A medicine label says: ‘Take two tablets with food, twice a day.’ How many tablets do you take in one day?
questions.options: Six | Four | One | Two
questions.explanation: Two tablets, twice a day: two in the morning and two in the evening makes four in one day. Reading a label carefully keeps you safe.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: The Body, Illness and the Clinic

questions.question: You ask for the bank. A man says: ‘Go along this street, past the market, and it is on the left.’ Where is the bank?
questions.options: Inside the market. | On the right, before the market. | Behind you. | On the left, after the market.
questions.correctAnswer: On the left, after the market.
questions.explanation: Past the market means you go beyond it, and on the left tells you which side. Following route words like along, past and left gets you there.

questions.question: The nurse speaks quickly and you do not understand. What is the best thing to say?
questions.options: It does not matter. | Speak English. | Could you say that again more slowly, please? | I understand everything.
questions.correctAnswer: Could you say that again more slowly, please?
questions.explanation: Asking someone to repeat or slow down is a skill, not a weakness. Could you and please make the request polite, and most people are glad to help.

questions.question: Choose the best word to complete the sentence: ‘It was raining hard, ______ I took a taxi.’
questions.options: because | so | who | the
questions.explanation: So introduces the result: the rain came first, so the taxi followed. Because would introduce the reason — I took a taxi because it was raining.

questions.question: Your new kettle stopped working after two days. What do you say at the shop?
questions.options: This kettle is broken. I would like a replacement, please. | This kettle is wonderful, thank you. | I am a kettle. | You broke my kettle yesterday.
questions.correctAnswer: This kettle is broken. I would like a replacement, please.
questions.explanation: Say what is wrong — it is broken — and then say what you want. Calm, clear words like these get problems fixed.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Getting Help and Getting Things Done

questions.question: Read: ‘Amina studies English every evening. Last week she introduced herself at a meeting, and next month she will present her work in English.’ What did Amina do last week?
questions.options: She missed the meeting. | She stopped studying English. | She presented her work. | She introduced herself at a meeting.
questions.correctAnswer: She introduced herself at a meeting.
questions.explanation: Last week points to the past, and the past verb introduced tells you what happened then. The presentation is next month — still in the future.

questions.question: A colleague asks: ‘Do you work on Saturdays?’ You do not. Which short answer is correct?
questions.options: No, I don’t work not. | No, I not. | No, I am not. | No, I don’t.
questions.explanation: A do question takes a do answer: Do you work? No, I don’t. Am and are answer questions that start with are you or is she.

questions.question: Read the message: ‘Would you like to join us for dinner on Friday? Let me know if you can come.’ What is the message doing?
questions.options: Complaining about dinner. | Refusing an invitation. | Inviting you to dinner. | Cancelling dinner.
questions.explanation: Would you like to join us is an invitation. The sender also asks you to reply — let me know — so a short answer back is the polite next step.
